title: Over-Generic Type Parameters (Complexity Inflation)
damaged_code:
```rust
fn process_any_data<T, U, V>(input: T) -> V
where
    T: IntoIterator<Item = U>,
    U: AsRef<str> + std::fmt::Debug,
    V: FromIterator<String>,
{
    // ...
    todo!()
}
```
pattern: Declaring excessively complex generic type parameters and trait bounds on helper functions to unify algorithms that are structurally similar but conceptually distinct.
why_bad: It makes the code unreadable and inflates the cognitive load of using or modifying the function. The compiler errors on trait bound mismatches become extremely difficult to debug, slowing down development.
detection: A function with 3 or more generic type parameters and complex trait bounds (e.g., 4 or more bounds in a `where` clause) used only for standard business logic workflows.
counterexample: Low-level library primitives or foundational mathematical/parsing crates where highly abstract generic algorithms are necessary for universal compatibility.
fix: Write separate, concrete, highly optimized functions for each specific domain type, or simplify the bounds by using concrete DTOs.
source: Titus Winters et al., *Software Engineering at Google* (2020), Chapter 13; Sandi Metz, *Practical Object-Oriented Design* (2019).
